entities.summary:
Mormonism, formally established as the Church of Christ by Joseph Smith in Fayette, New York, on April 6, 1830, is a distinct religious tradition and theology centered on the Book of Mormon as a companion scripture to the Bible. Originating in the "Burned-over District" of western New York during the Second Great Awakening, it quickly distinguished itself with claims of a restoration of primitive Christianity, new revelations, and a unique cosmology. This movement, often referred to as the Latter Day Saint movement, represents a significant American-born faith that dramatically shaped the demographic and cultural landscape of the American West, subsequently expanding into a global religious presence with millions of adherents worldwide.

Following its foundational period, Mormonism experienced intense persecution and internal schisms, leading to a series of westward migrations. After initial settlements in Kirtland, Ohio, and Missouri, the community established Nauvoo, Illinois, a thriving city that rivaled Chicago in population by the early 1840s. The assassination of its founder, Joseph Smith, and his brother Hyrum in Carthage, Illinois, in 1844 precipitated a succession crisis. Under the leadership of Brigham Young, the largest faction, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), embarked on an epic trek to the Great Basin, establishing Salt Lake City in 1847. There, they built a theocratic commonwealth, practiced plural marriage (polygamy) until its official cessation in 1890, and developed a complex system of temple ordinances and community life.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mormonism profoundly shaped the demographic and cultural development of the American West, leading to the creation of Utah and influencing subsequent religious freedom debates. It also grew into a major global faith with over 17 million adherents, demonstrating the enduring power of new religious movements.
